skip_reason: Outbound accounts-receivable and service-recovery call, not a sales conversation. Sergio (branch manager) called a past customer about a $1,295 shortfall on a completed August 2nd move — 'we noticed that they're still missing payment for your move that happened on August 2nd... it looks like the total came out to $3,170. But we only got payment for $1,875.' No move was being sold, quoted, or scheduled; the entire call is collections reconciliation that turned into a post-move service post-mortem on crew performance. The 85-pt Sales Call Scorecard does not apply.
items_missed: Not scored against the 85-pt rubric. The observations below are call-handling notes for a collections and service-recovery conversation, not scorecard deductions.

The opening framed the shortfall as the customer's non-payment before any facts were established: 'we noticed that they're still missing payment for your move... I don't know if you have any feedback for that move or what happened there, but it looks like the total came out to $3,170. But we only got payment for $1,875.' Sergio then compounded it with 'what was the reason we couldn't get the full payment?' and 'What happened on the move? That may you not pay the full amount.' The customer's reaction was immediate and correct: 'your guy agreed on the payment and I accepted it and nothing to do with mean refusing any kind of payment whatsoever. So, correct your verbiage right now.' The discount had been authorized internally by Einstein's own dispatcher; the record was incomplete, not the customer.

The internal check was run after the call rather than before it. Sergio had already spoken to Ron and to Alex in dispatch ('we talked to Ron who was a lien mover talked to Alex who's the manager there? Dispatching he did mentioned that the move did go long') and still opened as if the shortfall were unexplained. The write-off was authorized and knowable before dialing.

The customer had to ask twice what kind of conversation he was in before getting a straight answer: 'If this is not a discussion about how you're gonna try and get some more money from me then I'm happy to talk if this is a discussion about whether or not you should try, you're trying to get some more money from me then it's a little different discussion which one is it.' Sergio never answered it directly — he said he was 'trying to get clarification' — and the customer did not learn the balance was being written off until roughly twenty minutes in.

No service-recovery gesture was made. This is a customer who paid for a move where, by his account, a third of the apartment was left behind, the storage unit was never touched, and he carried items down himself: 'we left a probably a third of the house. That's how bad it was and I moved it with my cars.' He also raised a possible inventory shortfall — 'I think I'm missing several things. I think they didn't put stuff in the truck' — and that claim was never logged, never investigated, and never followed up on. No credit, no callback commitment, no claims handoff.
The reported missing-items concern in particular should have been routed to claims, not absorbed into a training conversation.

The call ran nearly thirty minutes with the customer speaking for the large majority of it. Sergio's contribution across long stretches is a bare 'Yeah,' repeated dozens of consecutive times. The substantive content he needed — crew pacing, no staging at the elevator, both movers leaving the floor together, the freight elevator not locked off — arrived in the first ten minutes; the remaining twenty produced industry anecdotes and stories about the customer's prior movers.

No future business was asked for, despite an unusually clear opening. The customer volunteered 'I probably will use you guys again' and Sergio's response ended the call rather than acting on it — no next move booked, no note that he would follow up, no direct line offered.
top_strength: Sergio recovered a call that opened hostile and ended it with a customer saying 'I probably will use you guys again,' and he did it by absorbing rather than defending. The customer opened by telling him to correct his verbiage and did not let up for ten minutes; Sergio never once pushed back, never justified the crew, and never tried to reclaim the money. He asked diagnostic questions instead, and good ones — 'You felt like the loading dock at the apartment was relatively close to the unit we had it available for like the full load uptime you feel like that wasn't like a cause of a going a little bit over. Cause it sounds like you're prepped, it sounds like you're ready to go but the guys were taking like fifteen minute trips which is a red flag' — which is a manager separating facility constraints from crew performance in real time, and which produced the most useful fact on the call: the crew could not lock the freight elevator and never staged in front of it. The turning point is the moment he stopped investigating and started owning it, unprompted and in full: 'usually for us a one bedroom takes around that three and a half, four and a half hours for it to be a ten hour load up is crazy. I think the biggest thing is we didn't set proper expectations like during the morning walkthrough or what the game plan is or anything like that, it kinda just went on and without proper communication with you and I feel like that discount is justified.' He validated his own company's write-off against an angry customer's account, named the specific process failure, and said the discount was correct — which is the sentence that ended the dispute. He then closed the loop on the internal side, explaining honestly that the crew was a five-year lead paired with a three-month hire ('Rodrick who is the lead mover with you has been with us for about five years and Desiree was probably in within three months'), committed to using it in training ('I have notes for this move that helps me follow up with next month's training'), and apologized for his own opening without excuses: 'I may have came on Monday morning a little bit tough, I apologize for that.' The customer apologized back. He also landed the estimate-accuracy point squarely and in the company's voice: 'it is an estimate but we want to be close to estimate as possible. We don't want it to just go way over almost double cause that's just crazy and I put myself in your issues.'
coaching_note: Scored as a skip — this is collections and service recovery, not a sales call, and the 85-pt scorecard does not apply. Three things are worth carrying forward anyway. First, the process fix, which is not really Sergio's to own: he was sent to collect a balance that his own dispatcher had already written off, and he found that out from the customer. The sequence has to be internal-first — reconcile with dispatch, confirm whether a field discount was authorized, and only then decide whether a customer call is warranted at all. If it is, it opens as 'I'm reviewing your August 2nd move because the total on the contract doesn't match what we billed you, and from what I've already heard internally the move ran long and our dispatcher adjusted it. I want to hear what happened from you' — not 'we're still missing payment.' Sergio recognized this himself by the end and apologized for it, which is to his credit, but he should not have been holding that bag. Second, and this one is a real gap: the customer said, on a recorded call, that he believes items were never loaded and that the storage unit portion of the job was never performed. That is a claims matter and it was never routed anywhere. It got a 'Yeah' and the conversation moved on to industry anecdotes. Any statement of possible missing property gets logged and handed to claims the same day, regardless of whether the customer is asking for anything. Worth checking whether anything was ever opened on this one. Third, the recovery itself is genuinely good and worth reusing: the pattern of listen fully, ask a diagnostic question that separates facility from crew, then own the specific process failure out loud and validate the discount, is what turned this call. The only refinement is timing — he reached it at roughly minute twenty, and the customer spent the preceding ten minutes not knowing whether he was in a dispute. Getting to 'the discount was right, I'm not here to reopen it, I'm here to find out what went wrong' inside the first two minutes would have produced the same outcome and the same crew intelligence in a third of the time. One operational note for the branch: by the customer's account a two-man crew took ten and a half hours on a 1,400 sq ft apartment against a typical three-and-a-half to four-and-a-half hour benchmark, left roughly a third of the load behind, and never touched the contracted storage stop — and the fix on the day was a dispatcher discount rather than a schedule intervention. Whatever the crew-pairing policy is for putting a three-month hire with a lead on a full apartment load, this job is a data point for it.
phone_presence_notes: Took ten minutes of genuine hostility without a single defensive word, kept asking rather than arguing, and ended with the customer apologizing to him and saying 'I probably will use you guys again' — the warmth is real and it is what saved the account; held back from a 5 by the opening, which he himself apologized for, and by long stretches where his entire contribution is a repeated bare 'Yeah.'
audio_review_reason: The customer holds roughly eighty percent of the airtime across thirty minutes and Sergio's side is largely single-word backchannel, which the transcript cannot distinguish between engaged active listening and disengaged filler — the score of 4 rests almost entirely on his two substantive passages. Audio is also needed on the first ninety seconds: the opening lines read as accusatory on the page and drew an immediate 'correct your verbiage right now,' and it matters for coaching whether the tone was blunt or merely the wording.
